title: Cases that pin down a crew rule

blocks.text: A tree-trimming contractor's planning model has a crew rule, and the rule has no tests. Jobs take one or more years of work and use a given number of crew-months in each of those years; each year has a fixed number of crew-months. With $`x_{j,s} = 1`$ when job $`j`$ starts in year $`s`$, and $`m_{j,k}`$ the crew-months job $`j`$ uses in its $`k`$-th year of work ($`k = 0, 1, \dots`$):
\sum_{j} \; \sum_{s \in T_j,\; 0 \le y - s < |m_j|} m_{j,\,y-s}\, x_{j,s} \;\le\; K_y \qquad \forall y \in \{2027, 2028, 2029\} \qquad \text{(crews}_y)

Your job is not to write the rule but to write the cases that test it. `cases()` returns a list of hand-made cases `(jobs, crews, plan, allowed)`; the comments in `crew_cases.py` give each field's shape. Each case should be small enough to check by eye: one or two jobs, and crew numbers chosen so that the crew rule decides.

The tests build a model with the crew rule alone for each case, fix the plan, and check your verdict, so every verdict must be the correct rule's, and your cases must hold at least one allowed and one refused plan. Then they run your cases against three wrong versions of the rule, each a mistake real code makes, and some case must catch each one, that is, get a different verdict from it than the one you wrote:

items: a rule written as if the limit were strict, so a year may use at most $`K_y - 1`$ crew-months;
a rule whose loop over the years stops one year early, so 2029 is never checked;
a rule that charges all of a job's crew-months to the year it starts.

blocks.text: Write the cases. About five lines.

"""Hand-made cases that pin down the crew rule of a tree-trimming contractor's model."""

from __future__ import annotations

YEARS = (2027, 2028, 2029)

# One case: (jobs, crews, plan, allowed)
#   jobs:    {job: (crew-months in each year of work, first allowed start, last allowed start)}
#   crews:   {year: crew-months available}, one entry for every year of YEARS
#   plan:    {job: start year}; a job not in the plan is not started
#   allowed: True if the crew rule accepts the plan, False if it refuses it


def cases() -> list[tuple[dict, dict, dict, bool]]:
    return [
        ({"oak": ((2,), 2027, 2027)}, {2027: 2, 2028: 2, 2029: 2}, {"oak": 2027}, True),
        ({"elm": ((3,), 2029, 2029)}, {2027: 5, 2028: 5, 2029: 2}, {"elm": 2029}, False),
        ({"ash": ((2, 2), 2027, 2027)}, {2027: 3, 2028: 3, 2029: 3}, {"ash": 2027}, True),
        ({"fir": ((5,), 2027, 2027)}, {2027: 4, 2028: 4, 2029: 4}, {"fir": 2027}, False),
    ]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for jobs, crews, plan, verdict in cases():
        print(plan, "allowed" if verdict else "refused")

cases.says: every case's verdict is the correct rule's, and the cases hold at least one allowed and one refused plan
a plan that uses every crew-month of a year is allowed, so a rule written as one month short fails it
a plan over the crews only in the plan's last year is refused, so a loop that stops a year early fails it
a job that works over two years fits month by month but not with all its months charged to its start year

origin.section: Pair Every Refused Plan With an Allowed One, at the Boundary

concepts: each refused plan is paired with an allowed one on either side of the rule's limit
a constraint is tested alone on a hand-made instance where it is the only rule that can bind
